sections.title: No cocoon, no pupa — just gradual change

blocks.x: Cockroaches belong to the order Dictyoptera and suborder Blattaria. Of roughly 4,000 known species, only about 50 have taken up residence as domestic pests. The name itself is inherited from the Latin blatta, "cockroach" — and in everyday speech they're just as often called roaches or steambugs.

blocks.cap: Side-by-side illustration comparing the Oriental, American and German cockroach

blocks.x: Not a direct transmitter — a carrier

Unlike mosquitoes and fleas, cockroaches aren't associated with disease by direct transmission. Instead, they harbour pathogens — typically those causing gastroenteritis — and deposit them indiscriminately on food and equipment simply by walking across them.
Warm, nocturnal, and unfussy about food

items: Cockroaches like warmth — by day they hide behind radiators and hot-water pipes.
They are nocturnal and rarely seen during daylight unless disturbed.
They are omnivorous, voracious feeders: paper, hair, excreta, shoes, cloth, dead insects and vegetables are all fair game.
They can survive 5–10 weeks without water and many months without food.

blocks.x: A cockroach's body is engineered for squeezing into cracks and surviving almost anything — a flattened, armoured chassis with sensory antennae up front and a pair of wing-cases folded like closed scissors on top.

sections.title: No cocoon, no pupa — just gradual change

blocks.x: Cockroaches develop by incomplete (hemimetabolous) metamorphosis: there is no pupal stage. A hatchling looks like a small, pale, wingless version of its parents, and simply grows and darkens with every moult.

blocks.cap: Cockroach life cycle diagram showing egg, several nymph stages, adult ready to fly, and adult, arranged in a circular cycle

blocks.x: The ootheca
Eggs are laid encased together in a brown, bean-shaped case or capsule called an ootheca — the roach's signature reproductive structure.
Hemimetabolous development
There is no pupal stage. Wingless or undeveloped nymphs hatch directly from the ootheca; young nymphs are pale and delicate, older ones progressively darker until they resemble the adult.

Cockroaches don't inject or bite — they contaminate. As they move between waste, drains and food, they can pick up and indiscriminately deposit bacteria, parasites, fungi and viruses, alongside triggering allergic disease from their own bodies and droppings.
Bacteria
Linked to dysentery, typhoid, pneumonia, tuberculosis and urticaria.
Parasites
Associated with iron-deficiency anaemia and biliary ascariasis.
Fungi
Linked to invasive infections and allergic reactions.
Viruses
Linked to Hepatitis A and meningitis.
Nematodes & an intermediate host role
Cockroaches are also known to serve as the intermediate host of the acanthocephalid Moniliformis moniliformis.
Allergies
Beyond microbial transmission, direct allergy to cockroaches or their dried fecal pellets is itself a recognised medical concern.
Effective control typically combines residual chemical treatment of harbourage sites with non-chemical approaches that reduce numbers without repeated pesticide use.
